auxiliary_material: The study utilized NanoString gene expression profiling and CyTOF mass cytometry on cryopreserved paired peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) collected longitudinally. Specific immune findings included decreased abundance scores of circulating macrophages (p=.018) and neutrophils (p=.035), and reduced circulating classical monocytes (p=.0059) in the high fiber arm versus control within week 5-8. T cell activation gene signatures were higher in the high fiber arm. These immune changes were more prominent in patients receiving combination nivolumab + ipilimumab compared to monotherapy, though subgroup sample sizes were small (n=3 vs n=7). The abstract notes that circulating monocyte levels are known to negatively correlate with ICB response.
outline_action: Use this study as primary evidence for the feasibility and immune-modulating effects of high-fiber dietary intervention in human ICI cohorts. Cite the FMT results to support the claim of microbiome dependence. However, explicitly note that the specific human microbiome compositional changes associated with efficacy are not detailed in this abstract, requiring reference to full-text publications or complementary studies to complete the 'microbiome change' link in the human causal chain. Plan to search for full-text reports of the DIET trial that may contain the 16S/metagenomic sequencing data of the human participants.
remaining_gap: The success criteria requires a human diet intervention trial reporting microbiome changes with ICI efficacy causal chain. While this study is a human diet intervention trial that establishes microbiome dependence via FMT and reports improved treatment outcomes, the supplied abstract does not explicitly detail the specific human microbiome composition changes (e.g., taxa abundance shifts) that correlated with efficacy within the human cohort itself; it primarily reports human immune profiling and uses mouse FMT to infer the microbiome's causal role. Therefore, the explicit human microbiome change data linked to efficacy remains unspecified in this text.
useful_material: This study conducted the Phase II Diet and Immune Effects Trial (DIET, NCT04645680), a randomized double-blinded dietary intervention in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Patients were randomized (2:1) to a high fiber diet (30-50 g/d) versus a healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors reported early results showing the intervention is feasible with promising improvements in treatment outcomes. While the primary human data focused on peripheral immune profiling (showing reduced circulating monocytes and increased effector-memory T cells in the high fiber arm), the study included translational human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) studies. In these FMT experiments, mice receiving stool from patients post-high fiber intervention demonstrated improved ICB response compared to pre-intervention stool, suggesting microbiome-dependent benefits. The authors conclude that the high fiber diet mediates regulation of peripheral immunity during immunotherapy in a microbiome-dependent manner.
